tier_reason: First-party timings hard-coded in cell 0 of Blur_algorithms py/performance.ipynb (arrays plotted to bench.png), produced by Source.cpp's Test() (cv::GaussianBlur vs pffft_, single-shot std::chrono). CPU is stated (Apple M3 Pro) but there is no build file, compiler, flags, OpenCV version or build, or thread count, so the tier is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Blur_algorithms README (repo archived 2024-12-26): 'how surprisingly fast is the 1D implementation in pffft compared to OpenCV that is the standard market reference', with linear versus exponential growth as size rises. py/performance.ipynb cell 0 holds hard-coded arrays in ms (pffft vs cv::GaussianBlur): 2000x1300 11.52 vs 107.43; 6500x4000 114.97 vs 1604.24; 12000x7300 433.94 vs 6317.43; 24000x14500 1728.56 vs 33509.56; at 1500x1000 OpenCV was faster, 24.97 vs 32.05. Derived from page data: pffft takes 9.0x (2500x1600) to 20.0x (23000x13900) less time at 45 of 46 sizes, and 0.78x at 1500x1000.
corrections.workload: True Gaussian blur of 3-channel 24-bit images with sigma = sqrt(image dimension), using pffft 1D separable FFT convolution in float32 tiles with reflect-101 padding, versus cv::GaussianBlur(image, image, Size(0,0), sigma) on 8-bit data. The notebook labels 46 sizes from 1500x1000 to 24000x14500; the commented-out loop in Source.cpp describes 45 sizes from 1500x1000 to 11400x7600. Apple M3 Pro, 12 cores.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 5 stars (LibGaussianBlur); 4 stars on archived Blur_algorithms; published on PyPI as gaussianblur 1.1.2 (2025-03-29)
corrections.caveats: The numbers live in the archived predecessor Blur_algorithms (no LICENSE file), not in LibGaussianBlur. LibGaussianBlur's src/gaussianblur.cpp keeps the same pffft ordered-transform tile convolution (pffft_sorted_optimized_convolution) but has never been benchmarked against OpenCV in its own repo. Each size was timed once (std::chrono printf in Source.cpp, no repetitions or warm-up). The pffft time at 1500x1000 (32 ms) is higher than at 2000x1300 (11.5 ms), which points to a cold-start cost in the first run. The size axis cannot be matched to the code. The commented-out benchmark loop in Source.cpp covers 45 sizes in 225x150 steps up to 11400x7600, calls cv::Size(y, x) so each image is 1000 wide by 1500 tall, and sets sigma = sqrt(x). The notebook labels 46 sizes in 500x300 steps up to 24000x14500, and the README says 45 images up to 11400x7600. The repo states no compiler, flags, OpenCV version or OpenCV build (IPP, NEON, threading backend). The FFT path is multi-threaded through hybrid_loop (OpenMP or std::thread, chosen by build macros), and nothing records which was used or how many threads OpenCV ran. The two sides compute different things. The FFT side convolves in float32, truncates the kernel at radius sigma*sqrt(2 ln 255) - 1 and clamps it to the largest image dimension. OpenCV runs its own direct separable 8-bit convolution with its own kernel-size rule. No accuracy comparison against OpenCV output is published. sigma = sqrt(width) gives kernels of hundreds of taps, the worst case for direct convolution. The result does not transfer to small sigma, and OpenCV won at the smallest size. A Gaussian blur is a filter, not resampling or colour conversion, so the fit to this category is borderline. The last commit is an automated coverage-badge update.

notes: Notebook numbers and the 9x-20x range are confirmed exactly (cell 0). The weak points are single-shot timing, unknown OpenCV build and threads, and a size axis that disagrees with the benchmark loop in Source.cpp. The measured algorithm is the same one LibGaussianBlur ships.

tier_reason: bench.sh and test.c wire Smolscale against libswscale, Pixman, stb_resize and GDK-Pixbuf, and the Makefile gives gcc with -O2, but the repo ships no results. The only numbers are absolute throughput figures from search snippets of the author's blocked blog post, so the tier is capped at C and no ratio against any baseline was seen.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No ratio against any baseline was seen. The repo (README, bench.sh, plot.sh, gnuplot/) ships no results. Snippets only, from the author's blog post 'Battle of the Bilerps: Image Scaling on the CPU' (2019-07-08; hpjansson.org is blocked here). One snippet says that on 8 threads Smolscale scaled a 16383x16383 image to a much smaller one in roughly 50 ms, about 5.3 gigapixels/s or ~21 GB/s of input. Another says the benchmarks ran on an i7-4770K (Haswell) at 3.5 GHz with a 2000x2000 RGBA input, with Smolscale MT averaging about 50 ms per frame. The per-library comparison plots in the post were not seen.
corrections.workload: Proportional scaling sweep (test.c run_benchmark_proportional) of a random 32-bit RGBA canvas from 0.01x up to 2x of the input size, so both downscaling and upscaling. The bench.sh defaults use 200 steps and 5 repetitions on 1920x1080 and 3840x2160 inputs (0.01-2x) and 7680x4320 (0.01-1x). TESTS_AVAILABLE adds sets such as 16383x16383 at 0.0001-0.1x. Each library runs its own filter: libswscale uses SWS_FAST_BILINEAR (scale <= 2) or SWS_AREA; Pixman uses separable box convolution (beyond 2x reduction) or bilinear; GDK-Pixbuf uses GDK_INTERP_BILINEAR; stb_image_resize uses a box filter in linear colorspace with premultiplied alpha.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc. Smolscale is built with -Wall -Wextra -g -O2 -DSMOL_WITH_AVX2, and smolscale-avx2.c additionally with -mavx2 (runtime dispatch). test.c is built at -O2, and Skia at -O3 when enabled. The baseline libraries (libswscale, Pixman, GDK-Pixbuf, SDL_gfx) are system packages found through pkg-config, so their build flags are the distro's.
corrections.hardware: i7-4770K (Haswell) at 3.5 GHz according to a search snippet of the blocked blog post; not stated in the repo
corrections.stars_or_usage: 39 stars; vendored into hpjansson/chafa (5.3k stars) as chafa/internal/smolscale
corrections.caveats: The evidence is snippet-only. The comparison numbers are in a blog post that could not be opened (egress blocked), so the speedup against each baseline is unconfirmed and the tier is capped at C. The public harness ships no results. Threading is asymmetric: 'Smolscale MT' (test.c scale_do_smol_threaded) runs a GThreadPool with g_get_num_processors() threads, while libswscale, Pixman, stb and GDK-Pixbuf are called single-threaded. The libraries also do different work, since each uses its own filter (fast bilinear or area, box convolution, bilinear, box in linear light), so quality differs. The README said at the time that the AVX2 file was 'mostly just a straight copy of the generic code'. The benchmark compares 2019-era library versions. The standalone repo's last commit is 2023-04-12, but the code is still developed inside Chafa (chafa/internal/smolscale, commits up to 2026-09-25), which is the maintained copy. The license is LGPLv3 or BSD 4-clause at the user's choice (COPYING). BSD-4-Clause is not OSI-approved, but the LGPLv3 option is.

notes: There is no comparative number anywhere reachable, only absolute throughput from snippets. C is kept per the snippet rule, but this is close to D. An enricher with blog access could add per-library ratios. Consider pointing users at Chafa's actively maintained copy.

corrections.hardware: Android phone(s), models not named; the README charts cover 6 phones of high, mid and low tier, also unnamed
corrections.caveats: The readable numbers come from screen recordings of the project's demo app (docs/assets/nv12_to_bgr.gif, bgr2rgba_with_mask.gif, Demo.gif). The FlyCV and OpenCV runs were recorded separately (on-screen clocks 20:05 and 20:03). The phone model, OpenCV version and build (NEON or carotene HAL, thread count), FlyCV thread count and compiler flags are not stated. The repo's benchmark/ code (Google Benchmark, e.g. benchmark/modules/img_transform/resize_bench.cpp) times FlyCV only and does not link OpenCV, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from public code. The 6-phone per-operator charts in the READMEs are hosted on user-images.githubusercontent.com and were not read; a reader with access could add per-operator ratios. The win for a single colour conversion is modest (1.16x for NV12 to BGR). Results measured on ARM phones may not carry over to x86. The last commit was 2023-06-02.
